stem: Garvey urged Black Americans to build their own businesses, ships, and institutions and to look toward a future nation in Africa. That program clashed most directly with leaders who urged Black Americans to

options.text: win full equality inside American institutions
return to farming in the rural South
options.misconception: Garvey's movement was urban and centered in Harlem, and his critics were urban too. Farming in the South was nobody's program in this debate.

options.text: leave politics to white reformers entirely
options.misconception: No Black leader of the 1920s urged leaving politics to white reformers. Both sides of the debate wanted Black action, not passivity.

options.text: adopt the culture of the Lost Generation writers
options.misconception: The Lost Generation writers were white expatriates in Paris. Their culture was not a program any Black leader offered.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the NAACP fought for inclusion and equality inside American life, while Garvey argued for separate Black institutions and a nation in Africa. The two programs pulled in opposite directions.
rationales.B: Garvey's movement was urban and centered in Harlem, and his critics were urban too. Farming in the South was nobody's program in this debate.
rationales.C: No Black leader of the 1920s urged leaving politics to white reformers. Both sides of the debate wanted Black action, not passivity.
rationales.D: The Lost Generation writers were white expatriates in Paris. Their culture was not a program any Black leader offered.
rationales.general:
1. Name Garvey's program: separate Black institutions and a future nation in Africa.
2. Ask what the opposite program would be: equality inside American institutions.
3. Ask who held that program. Background: the NAACP fought for inclusion and equality inside American life.
4. Name the clash: separatism against integration, inside one freedom struggle.
Remember: a debate has two sides with real programs, so find the program that pulls the other way.
